from PIL import Image
import colorsys
im = Image.open('barcode.png').convert('RGB')
w, h = im.size
px = im.load()

cols = []
for x in range(w):
    r = g = b = 0
    for y in range(h):
        p = px[x, y]
        r += p[0]; g += p[1]; b += p[2]
    cols.append((r/h, g/h, b/h))

def name_color(r,g,b):
    hh, ss, vv = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(r/255, g/255, b/255)
    if vv < 0.08: return "black"
    if ss < 0.12:
        if vv > 0.6: return "white/bright"
        return "gray"
    deg = hh*360
    if deg < 15 or deg >= 345: return "red"
    if deg < 40: return "orange"
    if deg < 65: return "yellow"
    if deg < 160: return "green"
    if deg < 200: return "cyan/teal"
    if deg < 260: return "blue"
    if deg < 320: return "purple"
    return "magenta/pink"

# Aggregate into 50 buckets of 20 columns
print("Timeline (each row = 2% of movie):")
for i in range(0, 1000, 20):
    bucket = cols[i:i+20]
    avg = tuple(round(sum(c[k] for c in bucket)/len(bucket)) for k in range(3))
    lum = 0.299*avg[0]+0.587*avg[1]+0.114*avg[2]
    names = {}
    for c in bucket:
        n = name_color(*c)
        names[n] = names.get(n, 0)+1
    top = sorted(names.items(), key=lambda kv:-kv[1])[:3]
    print(f"{i//10:>2}%  rgb={avg}  lum={lum:5.1f}  {top}")

# Dark fraction
dark = sum(1 for c in cols if 0.299*c[0]+0.587*c[1]+0.114*c[2] < 20)
print(f"\nDark(<20 lum) fraction: {dark/1000:.2%}")
EOF

***Take Me Home Tonight*** is a 2011 American [comedy-drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_drama "Comedy drama") film directed by [Michael Dowse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Dowse "Michael Dowse") and starring [Topher Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topher_Grace "Topher Grace") and [Anna Faris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Faris "Anna Faris") alongside [Dan Fogler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Fogler "Dan Fogler") and [Teresa Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Palmer "Teresa Palmer"). The screenplay was written by [Jackie and Jeff Filgo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_and_Jeff_Filgo "Jackie and Jeff Filgo"), former writers of the television sitcom *[That '70s Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That_'70s_Show "That '70s Show")*, of which Grace was a cast member. The film follows a recent college graduate who wants to change his career plans after his old high school crush invites him to a party. It was released to mixed reviews and was a [box-office bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box-office_bomb "Box-office bomb").

Shooting began on the week starting February 19, 2007,[\[5\]](#cite_note-Backstage-5) in [Phoenix, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona").[\[6\]](#cite_note-Collider-6) The film received its wide theatrical release on March 4, 2011 by [Relativity Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativity_Media "Relativity Media") in the United States, with [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") releasing in other territories.

The title comes from the 1986 [Eddie Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Money "Eddie Money") song [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(song\) "Take Me Home Tonight (song)"), also played in the theatrical trailer and on the menu screen of the Blu-ray and DVD releases. Despite having the same name, it never actually appears in the film.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Matt Franklin is a recent [MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") graduate, working at a Los Angeles [Suncoast Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suncoast_Video "Suncoast Video") store in 1988 while trying to figure out what he wants to do with his life, something that his [LAPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LAPD "LAPD") officer father has grown impatient with. When Matt's high school crush, Tori Frederking, walks into the store, he lies that he works at [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"). Tori invites Matt to a [Labor Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Day "Labor Day") party, hosted by Matt's twin sister Wendy's boyfriend, Kyle.

When Matt, Wendy, and Matt's best friend, Barry Nathan, head to the party, Barry steals a Mercedes-Benz convertible from the car dealership he got fired from earlier that day, saying Matt needs it to impress Tori. At the party, Matt awkwardly tries to woo her. Barry snorts some [cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine "Cocaine") he found in the glove box of the stolen car and gets involved in a dance-off, and Kyle [proposes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_proposal "Marriage proposal") to Wendy in front of everyone. Matt is disappointed she accepts, as he thinks Kyle will hold her back.

Tori takes Matt and Barry to her boss's party in [Beverly Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills "Beverly Hills"). Barry has a wild sexual encounter with Trish, an older woman, while Matt and Tori grow closer, after Matt's successful "put down" of Tori's boss, a habitual sexual harasser. They go into a neighboring backyard where they jump on a [trampoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trampoline "Trampoline"), play [truth or dare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_or_dare "Truth or dare"), and end up having sex.

Wendy shares her unopened admissions letter from [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") for graduate school with Kyle, and discovers she was not accepted. He is visibly relieved, while she is upset.

Matt confesses that he doesn't work at Goldman Sachs. Tori storms off, leaving him guilt-ridden. He finds Barry and they leave the party. Barry chastises Matt for not trying to have just one night of enjoyment and offers him a line of cocaine while driving. He tries to snort it, but ends up driving the convertible into a ditch. A police cruiser arrives, and it turns out to be Matt's dad.

Already disappointed with Matt's unwillingness to choose a career path, he further damages the convertible, coercing him to get a better job to pay off the damages. Matt apologizes for being such a failure, to which his dad replies that, as he's never tried, he has never really failed. His father just wants Matt to take a shot at something—*anything*—in life.

Knowing Tori has left her car at the party, Matt and Barry go back, where bets are being placed on who will "ride the ball", a giant, steel sphere that someone rides inside as it is rolled down a hill. Matt finds Tori and tries to apologize, but she is unwilling to forgive him.

Feeling he has nothing left to lose, Matt volunteers to "ride the ball". After making an impressive speech he gets inside it. Propelled down the hill, it ends up hitting several parked cars, flys off an embankment, and crashes through a wooden fence into a backyard swimming pool. Trapped inside and underwater, he almost drowns before escaping the sunken ball.

Barry rushes to the scene and is ecstatic to find Matt still alive. Walking arm in arm, they head back towards the party, and they meet up with Wendy and Tori, who are also elated to find him alive. Matt apologizes to Tori, she finally forgives him, and then gives him her phone number. They return to the party as dawn approaches. All who are still there cheer at Matt's successful return.

Wendy, realizing Matt was right, breaks up with Kyle, who experiences a crying breakdown. Barry—pondering his future while talking to Ashley, a Goth girl he met at the party, who tells him that maybe he should go to college—winds up sexually entangled with her. Outside, Matt boldly kisses Tori goodbye for the night because he still has her phone number to call.

Matt's dad, investigating the giant steel ball in the pool, smirks proudly when he finds, and then pockets, his son's name tag. Matt, Barry and Wendy stagger out of the party house, leaving together as the sun rises.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") was completed in 2007, but [Universal Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") shelved the film until its 2011 theatrical release.[\[7\]](#cite_note-deadline2010-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) Topher Grace posted that the release of the film was delayed when the studio did not know how to handle and promote a youth comedy film with portrayals of cocaine use, as the drug was prominent in the 1980s.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

Its release remained delayed until [Relativity Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativity_Media "Relativity Media") subsidiary [Rogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogue_Pictures "Rogue Pictures") acquired the film from [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") for $10 million.[\[3\]](#cite_note-LABox-3)[\[7\]](#cite_note-deadline2010-7) The film was previously titled *Young Americans* and *Kids in America*, titles of popular songs by [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie") and [Kim Wilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Wilde "Kim Wilde").[\[10\]](#cite_note-movieweb-10)

On March 3, 2011, while being interviewed on [Ryan Seacrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Seacrest "Ryan Seacrest")'s [102\.7 KIIS FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/102.7_KIIS_FM "102.7 KIIS FM") radio show, Topher Grace announced to former *[American Idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Idol "American Idol")* contestant [Chris Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Medina "Chris Medina") that 1% of the film's box office revenue would be donated to the care of Medina's injured fiancée, Juliana Ramos. Juliana was involved in a serious car accident in 2009 and suffered a traumatic brain injury. Her story has been widely followed across the nation since Medina's appearance on *American Idol*.

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film was released in the United States on March 4, 2011\. Relativity released a trailer for the film in December 2010\.

### Box office

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Box office")\]

*Take Me Home Tonight* was a box office flop. The film debuted at \#11, with $3,464,679 during its opening weekend in 2,003 theaters in North America. The film grossed $6,928,068 in North America, failing to recoup its $19 million budget.

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film holds a 27% approval rating based on 110 reviews with an average rating of 4\.60/10. The site's critical consensus reads, "It has a charming sweetness about it, but *Take Me Home Tonight* is neither funny nor original enough to live up to the comedies it evokes."[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the film has a score of 42 out of 100, based on 38 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews".[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Audiences surveyed by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film a grade C on scale of A to F.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)

[Peter Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Travers "Peter Travers") of *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* wrote that "*Take Me Home Tonight* has just enough heart and retro party spirit to hold the line before familiarity breeds contempt."[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) Critics have praised the leads and felt the film was heartwarming but was not very original or funny. [David Denby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Denby_\(film_critic\) "David Denby (film critic)") of *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")* wrote: "The movie is amiable enough: the young Australian actress Teresa Palmer is lovely and crisp, and the Canadian writer-director Michael Dowse manages the party traffic well."[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)

Colin Covert of the *[Minneapolis Star Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis_Star_Tribune "Minneapolis Star Tribune")* gave the film 3 out of 4 stars, writing that the movie is a "winning rag bag of gags, combining fast-paced physical shtick with a clever script. There's romantic comedy savvy period satire and "Jackass"-style stunts...*Take Me Home Tonight* is a time capsule from the heyday of [John Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hughes_\(filmmaker\) "John Hughes (filmmaker)") and [Cameron Crowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Crowe "Cameron Crowe"), a time when comedies allowed their characters to be human as well as humorous."[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

***Take Me Home Tonight*** is a 2011 American [comedy-drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_drama "Comedy drama") film directed by [Michael Dowse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Dowse "Michael Dowse") and starring [Topher Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topher_Grace "Topher Grace") and [Anna Faris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Faris "Anna Faris") alongside [Dan Fogler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Fogler "Dan Fogler") and [Teresa Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Palmer "Teresa Palmer"). The screenplay was written by [Jackie and Jeff Filgo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_and_Jeff_Filgo "Jackie and Jeff Filgo"), former writers of the television sitcom *[That '70s Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That_'70s_Show "That '70s Show")*, of which Grace was a cast member. The film follows a recent college graduate who wants to change his career plans after his old high school crush invites him to a party. It was released to mixed reviews and was a [box-office bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box-office_bomb "Box-office bomb").

Shooting began on the week starting February 19, 2007,[\[5\]](#cite_note-Backstage-5) in [Phoenix, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona").[\[6\]](#cite_note-Collider-6) The film received its wide theatrical release on March 4, 2011 by [Relativity Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativity_Media "Relativity Media") in the United States, with [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") releasing in other territories.

The title comes from the 1986 [Eddie Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Money "Eddie Money") song [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(song\) "Take Me Home Tonight (song)"), also played in the theatrical trailer and on the menu screen of the Blu-ray and DVD releases. Despite having the same name, it never actually appears in the film.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

Matt Franklin is a recent [MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") graduate, working at a Los Angeles [Suncoast Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suncoast_Video "Suncoast Video") store in 1988 while trying to figure out what he wants to do with his life, something that his [LAPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LAPD "LAPD") officer father has grown impatient with. When Matt's high school crush, Tori Frederking, walks into the store, he lies that he works at [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"). Tori invites Matt to a [Labor Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Day "Labor Day") party, hosted by Matt's twin sister Wendy's boyfriend, Kyle.

When Matt, Wendy, and Matt's best friend, Barry Nathan, head to the party, Barry steals a Mercedes-Benz convertible from the car dealership he got fired from earlier that day, saying Matt needs it to impress Tori. At the party, Matt awkwardly tries to woo her. Barry snorts some [cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine "Cocaine") he found in the glove box of the stolen car and gets involved in a dance-off, and Kyle [proposes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_proposal "Marriage proposal") to Wendy in front of everyone. Matt is disappointed she accepts, as he thinks Kyle will hold her back.

Tori takes Matt and Barry to her boss's party in [Beverly Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills "Beverly Hills"). Barry has a wild sexual encounter with Trish, an older woman, while Matt and Tori grow closer, after Matt's successful "put down" of Tori's boss, a habitual sexual harasser. They go into a neighboring backyard where they jump on a [trampoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trampoline "Trampoline"), play [truth or dare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_or_dare "Truth or dare"), and end up having sex.

Wendy shares her unopened admissions letter from [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") for graduate school with Kyle, and discovers she was not accepted. He is visibly relieved, while she is upset.

Matt confesses that he doesn't work at Goldman Sachs. Tori storms off, leaving him guilt-ridden. He finds Barry and they leave the party. Barry chastises Matt for not trying to have just one night of enjoyment and offers him a line of cocaine while driving. He tries to snort it, but ends up driving the convertible into a ditch. A police cruiser arrives, and it turns out to be Matt's dad.

Already disappointed with Matt's unwillingness to choose a career path, he further damages the convertible, coercing him to get a better job to pay off the damages. Matt apologizes for being such a failure, to which his dad replies that, as he's never tried, he has never really failed. His father just wants Matt to take a shot at something—*anything*—in life.

Knowing Tori has left her car at the party, Matt and Barry go back, where bets are being placed on who will "ride the ball", a giant, steel sphere that someone rides inside as it is rolled down a hill. Matt finds Tori and tries to apologize, but she is unwilling to forgive him.

Feeling he has nothing left to lose, Matt volunteers to "ride the ball". After making an impressive speech he gets inside it. Propelled down the hill, it ends up hitting several parked cars, flys off an embankment, and crashes through a wooden fence into a backyard swimming pool. Trapped inside and underwater, he almost drowns before escaping the sunken ball.

Barry rushes to the scene and is ecstatic to find Matt still alive. Walking arm in arm, they head back towards the party, and they meet up with Wendy and Tori, who are also elated to find him alive. Matt apologizes to Tori, she finally forgives him, and then gives him her phone number. They return to the party as dawn approaches. All who are still there cheer at Matt's successful return.

Wendy, realizing Matt was right, breaks up with Kyle, who experiences a crying breakdown. Barry—pondering his future while talking to Ashley, a Goth girl he met at the party, who tells him that maybe he should go to college—winds up sexually entangled with her. Outside, Matt boldly kisses Tori goodbye for the night because he still has her phone number to call.

Matt's dad, investigating the giant steel ball in the pool, smirks proudly when he finds, and then pockets, his son's name tag. Matt, Barry and Wendy stagger out of the party house, leaving together as the sun rises.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") was completed in 2007, but [Universal Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") shelved the film until its 2011 theatrical release.[\[7\]](#cite_note-deadline2010-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) Topher Grace posted that the release of the film was delayed when the studio did not know how to handle and promote a youth comedy film with portrayals of cocaine use, as the drug was prominent in the 1980s.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

Its release remained delayed until [Relativity Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativity_Media "Relativity Media") subsidiary [Rogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogue_Pictures "Rogue Pictures") acquired the film from [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") for $10 million.[\[3\]](#cite_note-LABox-3)[\[7\]](#cite_note-deadline2010-7) The film was previously titled *Young Americans* and *Kids in America*, titles of popular songs by [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie") and [Kim Wilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Wilde "Kim Wilde").[\[10\]](#cite_note-movieweb-10)

On March 3, 2011, while being interviewed on [Ryan Seacrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Seacrest "Ryan Seacrest")'s [102\.7 KIIS FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/102.7_KIIS_FM "102.7 KIIS FM") radio show, Topher Grace announced to former *[American Idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Idol "American Idol")* contestant [Chris Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Medina "Chris Medina") that 1% of the film's box office revenue would be donated to the care of Medina's injured fiancée, Juliana Ramos. Juliana was involved in a serious car accident in 2009 and suffered a traumatic brain injury. Her story has been widely followed across the nation since Medina's appearance on *American Idol*.

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release")\]

The film was released in the United States on March 4, 2011\. Relativity released a trailer for the film in December 2010\.

### Box office

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Box office")\]

*Take Me Home Tonight* was a box office flop. The film debuted at \#11, with $3,464,679 during its opening weekend in 2,003 theaters in North America. The film grossed $6,928,068 in North America, failing to recoup its $19 million budget.

### Critical response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Take_Me_Home_Tonight_\(film\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Critical response")\]

On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film holds a 27% approval rating based on 110 reviews with an average rating of 4\.60/10. The site's critical consensus reads, "It has a charming sweetness about it, but *Take Me Home Tonight* is neither funny nor original enough to live up to the comedies it evokes."[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the film has a score of 42 out of 100, based on 38 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews".[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) Audiences surveyed by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film a grade C on scale of A to F.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)

[Peter Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Travers "Peter Travers") of *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* wrote that "*Take Me Home Tonight* has just enough heart and retro party spirit to hold the line before familiarity breeds contempt."[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) Critics have praised the leads and felt the film was heartwarming but was not very original or funny. [David Denby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Denby_\(film_critic\) "David Denby (film critic)") of *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")* wrote: "The movie is amiable enough: the young Australian actress Teresa Palmer is lovely and crisp, and the Canadian writer-director Michael Dowse manages the party traffic well."[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)

Colin Covert of the *[Minneapolis Star Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis_Star_Tribune "Minneapolis Star Tribune")* gave the film 3 out of 4 stars, writing that the movie is a "winning rag bag of gags, combining fast-paced physical shtick with a clever script. There's romantic comedy savvy period satire and "Jackass"-style stunts...*Take Me Home Tonight* is a time capsule from the heyday of [John Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hughes_\(filmmaker\) "John Hughes (filmmaker)") and [Cameron Crowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Crowe "Cameron Crowe"), a time when comedies allowed their characters to be human as well as humorous."[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)
